<!-- https://www.crosswalknyc.com/digital-twins-glossary.html -->

# The words we use for digital twins, synthetic data and the panel.

Plain, one-line definitions of the 39 terms we use. A twin is an audience you can ask. An archetype is one group inside it. A seat is the person who speaks for that group in a room. The count adds up the real people behind each answer, and every count says how firm it is. The words also show what makes Crosswalk's twins different: they are behavior-built, counted in real people, and scored in public.

Updated November 2026 · Crosswalk Technologies, Inc. · Read the methodology

**Digital twin**
A live copy of a real audience that you can ask questions. Crosswalk builds one from 5+ years of what 10 million opted-in US people did, not from surveys or a chatbot. Read what a digital twin audience is.

**Twin**
Short for digital twin. An audience you can ask, built from 5+ years of what its people did. A twin can be a show's viewers, a service's subscribers, a star's followers, a brand's buyers, or a group you shape.

**Archetype**
One group inside a twin, such as "older regulars on sport and crime series" or "parents who stopped after the season ended." A twin has at least 12 archetypes, found by sorting the audience by where people are with the subject and by age. Together they add up to the whole audience.

**Archetype representative**
The person who stands for one archetype inside a twin, with a name, an age, a city and a bio. Each twin has at least 12. In a room, the archetype representative answers in character from what its people did.

**Seat**
The landing spot for each archetype representative in a room. A seat has a bio and a memory. It remembers what it said earlier in the room and in past rooms you have used it in.

**Room**
A focus group with one seat for each archetype, so never fewer than 12 seats. You never pick the number; the audience decides it. Read how an AI focus group works.

**Focus Group IQ**
The part of Digital Twins IQ where you open a room on a twin and ask it anything. Each room comes back as a CSV and a PDF with every question, split, read and voice.

**Predictive Analytics**
Bring one business question. Prometheus plans 5 to 8 questions from wide to narrow, runs the room for you, and hands back a verdict with a full report. Planning is free.

**Pilot Testing**
The room watches your cut from start to finish: a pilot, an episode, an ad, a feature or a run of episodes. Seats turn a dial as they watch, react on the clock, answer questions at the turns of the story, and fill out a scorecard at the end.

**The count**
The share, and the number of people, behind each answer. Each answer carries the people behind its seat, so a seat standing for 16.6 million people counts for more than one standing for 3.6 million. Shares add to 100% and people add to the room.

**How firm**
The word on every count: firm, leaning or early, with a range around it. Firm is within about 5 points, leaning within about 12, early up to about 20. The room always makes the call; the word says how firm it is.

**Range**
How far the real number could sit from the count, shown as a low and a high. A count of 63.1% with a range of 51.2% to 75.0% is leaning.

**Verdict**
The answer to a business question at the end of a Predictive Analytics run: yes, lean yes, lean no, no, split, or the winning option, with the numbers behind it, why, who drove it, what would change it, and what to ask next.

**The dial**
The 0 to 100 line each seat turns while it watches a cut. It goes up when a scene lands and down when a scene drags, confuses or loses the seat. A reading every 2 seconds on a short cut and every 4 on a long one.

**Reaction**
A moment marked on the clock by a seat: loved it, laughed, leaned in, lost, checked out or wow, each with its second and a line in the seat's own words.

**Scorecard**
The card every seat fills out after a cut: overall rating, would recommend, would finish the episode, would watch a second episode, how soon, and against expectations. Each share counts the people behind the seats and carries a range, with a word for how firm it is.

**Total positive**
Everyone who rates a cut excellent or very good. One of the four numbers at the top of a scorecard, next to excellent, definitely recommend and would finish.

**The norm**
What tests of the same kind usually score. You pick it, from all pilots to one genre such as procedurals. A genre gets its own norm once enough of its tests are on file.

**Dead spot**
The second where the room's dial sank the most during a cut. The favorite moment is the strongest good reaction in the room.

**Track record**
The public record of every call the twins made before its outcome, dated and never changed after, then scored when the result landed. Few research vendors publish one, and fewer keep their misses on it. See the record.

**Call**
A forecast or a room count with a real result to check against, put on the record before the result exists: the question, the audience, the figure and its range, the day the result is due and what will settle it. A call is never rewritten.

**Miss**
How far a call was off once the result landed. On a count, the share of the figure that happened. On a split, the points that would have to move for the two to match. On a winner, whether the side called was the side that won.

**Behavioral panel**
A group of people who agree to have what they do online recorded by software, so researchers can count real behavior instead of asking about it. Crosswalk's panel has 30 million opted-in people worldwide, 10 million in the US. Read what a behavioral panel is.

**Single source**
One person, one ID, every screen. The same person's phone, laptop and TV are counted together, so a search in the morning can be tied to a signup that night.

**Census matched**
The US panel's mix of ages, genders, regions and the rest matches the country's, so every answer scales from the panel to 329.9 million Americans the way a census sample does.

**Projected US people**
A panel count scaled up to the US population. When a read says 6,184,372 US viewers, that is the panel's count projected to the country, each person counted once.

**Penetration**
The share of an audience that did something: watched a service, bought a brand, searched a term. Always stated with its base.

**Index**
How an audience compares to the US population, where 100 is the average American. An index of 683 means 6.8 times as common as among most people.

**T+1**
Yesterday's behavior is on file today. The panel refreshes every morning.

**Synthetic data**
Data that was produced rather than observed. At Crosswalk, the outcomes a twin produces when you run a plan it has never seen: new data, built on real behavior. Read synthetic data in market research.

**Synthetic audience**
The twins a plan would reach, sized, described and projected to the US population. Made of the archetypes, at least 12, that add up to the whole audience.

**Synthetic respondent**
A program that answers a survey as if it were a person. Most are built from past surveys or from a language model playing a type of person. Crosswalk's archetype representatives answer from behavior instead. Read the comparison.

**Behavior-built twin**
A twin built from what real people did, not from what they said. It can be scored against what people do next. Every Crosswalk twin is behavior-built. Read the comparison.

**Interview-built twin**
A twin built from a long interview with one person, so it can answer later surveys the way that person would. It knows one conversation, not years of behavior.

**Chatbot persona**
A language model told to answer as a type of person, such as "a mother of two in Ohio." It is fast and cheap, but it has never met your audience and can change its answer each time.

**Census-built population**
Made-up people given real census traits, such as zip code, age, income and job. It matches the country's shape but has never watched a show or paid for one.

**Prometheus**
Crosswalk's research assistant. Ask it any audience question in plain English and it answers from what 10 million US people do. Ask it to build a twin, open a room, or explain a read.

**Digital Twins IQ**
Crosswalk's digital twin product, also called Twin IQ: the twins, Focus Group IQ, Predictive Analytics and Pilot Testing, with the public track record. See Digital Twins IQ.

**Crosswalk**
Crosswalk Technologies, Inc., Malibu, California. An opted-in behavioral panel of 30 million people worldwide, 10 million in the US, read through Prometheus and the IQ reports. Clients receive group statistics; no individual is identified.

Source: https://www.crosswalknyc.com/digital-twins-glossary.html

# How Prometheus works.

What it is built on, how it computes an answer, and why no other data source can beat it.

_How Prometheus works: the data, the record, a real answer, the breadth, and why it is different. Five minutes._

## Behavioral data on 30 million digital lives.

Not a survey and not a model. Crosswalk holds the record of what real people do online: 30 million opted-in people around the world, 10 million of them in a US panel that is census matched to the country. For each person, their entire digital life across every screen, under one ID, kept day by day since January 2021. That record is what Prometheus answers from.

**Behavioral**
What people search, watch, stream, buy, subscribe to and cancel. Observed, not asked.

**Longitudinal**
The same people in the panel day to day and year after year. Their behavioral data evolves daily and the record of their history remains intact.

**Every screen**
Phone, laptop, connected TV, tablet, game console. One person, one ID, one ordinary day in order with the time of day.

**Projected**
Every answer scales from the panel to the US population the way a census sample does, in percentages and in people.

## Ask Prometheus. It answers from that record.

Every answer is read from the longitudinal behavior of the people who fit your question or cohort, and it lands as an Excel file or a full PowerPoint deck.

### You ask.

Any question, in plain English. Type it or say it.

### Prometheus reads the record.

It finds the people who fit your query, reads five years of what they did, and calculates the answer. A quick count takes seconds. A full read, a few minutes.

### You get the answer.

Percentages and people, scaled up to the country. Download it as an Excel file, or export a full PowerPoint deck, rich with high-level insights and analysis that tell you how to make the data actionable. Ask it to email you the file, to cut the audience, or simply to move on to the next question.

## Who watches Landman, and what do they buy?

One question, asked as written. The answer came back in about three minutes: 6,184,372 US viewers, half of them 35 to 54, and just over 50% men. Their buying is everyday grocery and family goods first, and the delta against the average American sits in workwear, trucks and hardware. A marketing plan in one answer.

People who watched a Landman title in the window, counted once each and projected to the country. 31.6% are 35 to 44; only 2.1% are over 65.

Of purchase signals are grocery, family and CPG, at 79.4% penetration. The lift is Carhartt, Wrangler, Tractor Supply, AutoZone, Yeti and Home Depot.

Finish the season, and 48.0% watch with a second screen in hand: phone-led, same-session buying.

## Nine types of answers, and the digital twins.

The syndicated reports: one question each, the same ten million people behind all of them.

Go beyond the syndicated reports menu. Test a plan, a title, a price, or a product launch on ten million twins built from real behavior before you spend. See how Digital Twins IQ works, or read the methodology.

## Built on what people do, not what they say.

Every other source sees one slice of a life, or asks people to remember. Prometheus sees the whole person, ten million times over, and it answers in minutes.

## On every page, on your desktop, and in your API.

Type to it or talk to it. The same brain answers wherever you are.

### The dashboard.

Prometheus floats on every page. Open a profile and ask about it; the query knows what you are looking at.

A standalone Prometheus app, same account, same balance, same library, without opening a browser.

Your own tools ask the same questions and get the same files, with one key and one wallet.

From the question to the file, projected to the country. Before: a brief, a vendor, six weeks and a survey of what people remember.

## Prometheus, in plain words.

### What is Prometheus?

Crosswalk's research assistant. You ask a question about an audience, and it answers from the actual behavior of 10 million US people in the Crosswalk panel: what they search, watch, stream, buy, subscribe to and cancel, recorded day by day since 2021.

### What can I ask it?

Anything about an audience. Who watches a title and what they buy. Which titles bring a service new subscribers. How people got from a clip to a purchase. Which touchpoint on a campaign moved them. What a sponsorship is worth. The nine syndicated reports are the menu, not the limit.

### How fast is it?

A quick count comes back in seconds. A full read, such as a complete audience profile, takes a few minutes and lands in your dashboard as a file you can download or email.

### How is this different from a survey or a ratings service?

Surveys tell you what people say and can recall. Ratings see one screen, web analytics; one site, credit card data; one checkout. Prometheus reads one person across all of it, ten million times over, census matched and refreshed every morning, and its answers are checked against real outcomes rather than more surveys.

No. The panel is opted in, identity is kept apart from behavior, and Prometheus never answers about one person. Clients receive group statistics projected to the US population.
